title: The Overcounting Dichotomy of the Ordinary-Derivative Multiplicity Test
description: The parent entry (factor-remainder-hasse-derivative-fq) shows that over a characteristic-p field the ordinary iterated-derivative multiplicity test is reliable up to order p−1 and identically blind from order p on, and leaves open: quantify the overcounting for a GENERAL polynomial — the gap between the multiplicity the ordinary derivatives certify and the true (Hasse) multiplicity at a root. This entry answers it with a sharp dichotomy. Define the ordinary-certified multiplicity as the largest n with (derivative^[j] f)(a) = 0 for all j < n. Using the evaluation form of the scaling identity, (derivative^[k] f)(a) = (k! : F)·(hasseDeriv k f)(a), the outcome splits cleanly on the true multiplicity m := rootMultiplicity a f: if m < p the ordinary test is EXACT (certifies precisely m, gap 0); if m ≥ p it overcounts WITHOUT BOUND (every ordinary derivative vanishes at a, certifying every multiplicity). There is no intermediate regime — the test is either perfectly exact or infinitely wrong, and the switch happens precisely at m = p. Both regimes are realized concretely (X^p unbounded, a linear factor X − a exact). 8 theorems, 0 axioms, 0 sorries.

originalContributions: iterate_derivative_eval_eq: the evaluation form of the parent scaling identity, (derivative^[k] f).eval a = (k! : F) * (hasseDeriv k f).eval a. This is the bridge that lets the factorial threshold (k! : F) = 0 ↔ p ≤ k control the VALUES of the ordinary derivatives at a point, not just the whole polynomials.

unbounded_overcount: the m ≥ p regime. If (X − a)^p ∣ f then (derivative^[j] f).eval a = 0 for EVERY order j — split on the factorial threshold (blind for j ≥ p, Hasse-vanishing times j! for j < p). The ordinary test certifies arbitrarily large multiplicity: unbounded overcount.

ordinary_exact_below_threshold: the m < p regime. If the true multiplicity is exactly m < p, the ordinary derivatives vanish at a for all j < m and (derivative^[m] f).eval a ≠ 0 (since m! is a unit, promoting the first nonvanishing Hasse value). The ordinary test first fails at order m, certifying exactly m: gap 0.

overcounting_dichotomy: the capstone. For any f ≠ 0, phrased through the true rootMultiplicity a f, EXACTLY ONE of the two regimes holds — exact (m < p) or unbounded overcount (m ≥ p) — with the transition sharp at m = p. There is no intermediate overcounting regime.

relatedProblems.relationship: Parent: pins down the full failure profile (exact threshold (k! : F) = 0 ↔ p ≤ k; reliable up to p−1, blind from p) and asks, as its first open question, to quantify the overcounting for a general polynomial. This entry answers it with a sharp exact/unbounded dichotomy keyed to the true multiplicity m relative to p.

Provides the characteristic-free Hasse multiplicity factor theorem pow_X_sub_C_dvd_iff_hasseDeriv_eval_eq_zero: (X − a)^k ∣ f ↔ ∀ m < k, (hasseDeriv m f)(a) = 0. This entry uses that criterion to translate the true multiplicity m into the pointwise vanishing of Hasse (hence, via the k! factor, ordinary) derivatives.

overview.historicalContext: The multiplicity form of the Factor Theorem says, over a field of characteristic zero, that (X − a)^k ∣ f iff f and its first k−1 ordinary derivatives f^{(j)} = derivative^[j] f vanish at a. In positive characteristic the criterion breaks: over 𝔽_p, derivative(X^p) = 0, so the ordinary derivatives can all vanish while the multiplicity is large. Hasse's divided-power derivative repairs the criterion. The parent entry quantifies the breakdown qualitatively — a sharp cutoff at order p — and asks the natural quantitative follow-up: for a GENERAL polynomial, how far apart are the multiplicity the ordinary derivatives certify and the true (Hasse) multiplicity at a root?
overview.problemStatement: Over a field of characteristic p, fix f ≠ 0 and a root a of true multiplicity m := rootMultiplicity a f. Let the ordinary-certified multiplicity be the largest n such that (derivative^[j] f)(a) = 0 for all j < n. Determine the gap between the certified value and m. Show the gap is governed entirely by whether m reaches the characteristic p.
overview.proofStrategy: Everything runs through the evaluation form of the parent scaling identity: evaluating derivative^[k] f = (k! : F) • hasseDeriv k f at a gives (derivative^[k] f)(a) = (k! : F)·(hasseDeriv k f)(a) (iterate_derivative_eval_eq, via smul_eq_C_mul, eval_mul, eval_C). The Hasse multiplicity criterion pow_X_sub_C_dvd_iff_hasseDeriv_eval_eq_zero turns divisibility (X − a)^k ∣ f into the pointwise vanishing of the first k Hasse derivatives at a. Case m ≥ p: from (X − a)^p ∣ f, split on the factorial threshold — for j ≥ p the whole ordinary derivative is 0 (parent blindness), for j < p the Hasse value vanishes and the ordinary value is j! times it, so every ordinary derivative vanishes at a (unbounded_overcount). Case m < p: (X − a)^m ∣ f gives vanishing Hasse values below m (hence vanishing ordinary values), while (X − a)^{m+1} ∤ f forces the m-th Hasse value nonzero; since m! is a unit below p, the m-th ordinary value is nonzero, so the test first fails at m (ordinary_exact_below_threshold). The capstone overcounting_dichotomy splits on lt_or_ge m p and feeds le_rootMultiplicity_iff into the two lemmas.
keyInsights: The whole dichotomy is the evaluation form of one identity: (derivative^[k] f)(a) = (k! : F)·(hasseDeriv k f)(a). The ordinary VALUE at a is the Hasse value scaled by k!, so pointwise information loss is exactly the vanishing of the scalar (k! : F).

The true multiplicity m is the first order at which the Hasse value at a is nonzero. Whether the ordinary test can SEE that first nonzero order depends only on whether m < p (so m! is a unit) — the sharp threshold from the parent, now read pointwise.
m < p ⇒ EXACT: the m-th ordinary value equals m!·(nonzero Hasse value) ≠ 0, so the ordinary test fails at exactly m, matching the truth. Gap 0.

m ≥ p ⇒ UNBOUNDED overcount: below p the Hasse values already all vanish (they vanish below m ≥ p), and from p on the ordinary derivative is identically 0. So every ordinary derivative vanishes at a and the test certifies every multiplicity.

There is no middle ground. The gap is either 0 or ∞, and the switch is exactly at m = p — the qualitative cutoff of the parent becomes a quantitative all-or-nothing statement about a general polynomial.

sections.title: The Dichotomy and Its Two Realizations

conclusion.summary: A fully verified (0 sorries, 0 axioms, no native_decide) file of 190 lines and 8 theorems answering the parent's first open question. Over a field of characteristic p, the gap between the multiplicity the ordinary iterated-derivative test certifies at a root and the true (Hasse) multiplicity m is governed entirely by whether m reaches p: if m < p the ordinary test is EXACT (gap 0), and if m ≥ p it overcounts WITHOUT BOUND (certifies every multiplicity). The switch is sharp at m = p, and both regimes are realized concretely by X^p and by a linear factor X − a.
conclusion.implications: This upgrades the parent's qualitative cutoff (reliable to p−1, blind from p) into a quantitative all-or-nothing statement about an arbitrary polynomial: the overcounting gap is never a finite positive number — it is either 0 or ∞. Practically, ordinary derivatives read low-order multiplicities in characteristic p exactly right, but the moment a root's multiplicity reaches the characteristic the naive test loses all information at once, pinpointing exactly where the Hasse refinement becomes indispensable (e.g. separability/inseparability detection).
openQuestions: In the unbounded regime m ≥ p, stratify further by the base-p digits of m: which higher Hasse derivatives remain the FIRST nonvanishing ones, and how does the ordinary test's blindness interact with the Lucas/Kummer structure of the binomial coefficients defining hasseDeriv?

Transport the dichotomy to the truncated jet algebras F[X]/(X^n), where only finitely many Hasse derivatives are visible, and determine at which truncation length the exact/unbounded distinction becomes undecidable from the visible data.
